videos.title: How a lesson works
videos.transcript: Good morning. This is Stand Up. Here is how a lesson works. One idea. One sitting. About nine minutes. That's it. Then you write. Five minutes. It's saved only in this browser. Three questions. A study aid, not a test. Look again at the ones you missed. Done? Mark it done. Not ready? Skip it, come back. No hurry. Stand Up. Education, not advice.

videos.title: Pick up where you left off
videos.transcript: Close the tab. Life happens. Right? Come back, and the page remembers where you were. Saved in this browser. One click. Straight back to your lesson. Stand Up. Get up. Pick it up again.

videos.title: Your own pace
videos.transcript: Your start date. Your pace. Pick a day, or start today. Every date counts from there. Twelve weeks is a suggestion. Nothing locks. There are no deadlines. Ahead. On track. A bit behind. No deadlines. Your pace. Nothing locks. Stand Up.

videos.title: Out of ten, I failed nine
videos.transcript: In his own count, Jose has failed at nine of the ten things he's tried. In his twenties he started a digital advertising agency. He thought it would do very well. It didn't work out. But he never told himself he'd never use it again. Even when it fails, he said, it becomes part of your skill set. Years later, he ran a fishing tourism business. Digital advertising was how he got his clients to come. So here's the question. What did one of your failures give you that you still use?

videos.title: It’s just a feeling
videos.transcript: Jose once asked his class to stop and answer one question. How do you define love? When he was in high school, he visited his grandparents. One read the paper on one side of the room, the other on the other side. Day after day, for years. One day he asked them how they define love. They laughed. It's just a feeling, they said. They felt each other's presence. That was all. They weren't overly loving people, he said. They came from the Great Depression. So how much of that shapes us? How would you answer your grandparents' question?

videos.title: Pick one, then finish it
videos.transcript: Nobody has time. Or so we say. Jose heard it differently. When someone tells him they don't have time, he hears something else: I don't know how to manage my time. I don't know how to delegate. I don't know how to build a structure. His own lesson came from swimming. He swam for years, hours a day, before school and after. To get good at one thing, he said, you pick one. You can't be good at three or four at once. And once you finish one thing, you learn how you got there: the discipline, the goals, the process. Even if you leave that field, you keep the roadmap. So here's the question. What did you start and leave unfinished? What would finishing it have taught you?

videos.title: Is it conviction or fantasy?
videos.transcript: How many of us could lose money for five years and still say: I'm going to make it? Jose asked a harder question. Where is the line where you say: I made a wrong call? And where is the line where you say: no, my conviction is right? He calls the danger getting drunk on your own idea. You are inspired, and you stop watching the basics. Ego without logic brings you down. In his twenties he ignored the margins. Sales and volume looked great. The margins weren't there. His fix: ask people who know the field. Not an uncle in a different business. People who've done it. Write one project where you're losing money or time. Then write why you think it will work.

videos.title: Your three numbers
videos.transcript: Three numbers. Miss one, and an investor can end the meeting. Your burn rate. Your cost to get a customer. Your margin. Jose knows people living in what he calls the fantasy world. I have massive margins. Massive how much? Then he looks at the industry. Is the market growing or shrinking? Is your piece getting bigger? And before a joint venture he does one thing first. He reads their financials. Then he calls. Ask like an owner, and people see you differently. You care about their company's health. Write your three numbers. Then write the ones you don't know yet.

videos.title: Ask why not
videos.transcript: Delete one sentence from your vocabulary: that can't be done. Jose pointed to a founder who doesn't seem to have it. Told something is impossible, he asks: why not? And then he keeps asking. Jose's question for us: are you repeating your goal, with positive emotion, every day? Or does it still feel unfamiliar? A million in six months feels like a threat when it's unfamiliar. After six months of picturing it in detail, it feels possible. We build thought habits the way we build any habit. Specific. Measurable. Repeated. Write one goal. Say it every day this week. Then write what in your week doesn't line up with it.

videos.title: Where did my process break down?
videos.transcript: Blame feels good. For about a minute. Jose noticed that the leader they were studying doesn't blame anybody. Not people. Not circumstances. If you keep blaming outside things, Jose said, you have an inside problem. The question strong leaders ask: where did my process break down? Blame hands your power away. Auditing your process gets it back. In a small company it starts at the top. The leader takes accountability, and then everyone does. Focus on the problem. What are my options? When have I been here before? Write something that went wrong. Write who you were tempted to blame.
